sketches.title: Shed Law
sketches.premise: Two rival shed-keepers build strange little laws out of toolbox objects. On your turn, name one standing object that defeats the previous object by changing what it can do; then the shed’s Grand Inspector decides whether your law holds.
sketches.criterion: A move beats the standing object when its ordinary function plainly restrains, breaks, traps, cuts, joins, or otherwise directly changes that object, but merely hiding from it, surviving it, using a larger copy, or naming a nearby cousin does not count.
sketches.move_shape: Say what object you are and how it acts on the last one: “I am a padlock; I shut the toolbox that contains the hammer.”
sketches.first_card: Hammer: heavy-headed, swinging, and ready to make a problem look nailed down.

sketches.title: Toolbox Tug
sketches.premise: A toolbox becomes a tiny theater of contests: each player sends one tool onto the bench, and the next tool must answer it with a clear practical advantage. The host announces every upset as if a broom has challenged a dragon.
sketches.criterion: The new tool must directly prevent, undo, redirect, or disable what the previous tool does; dodging, merely lasting longer, and offering a bigger or fancier version of the same tool lose, while a different tool from the same family needs a specific mechanism.
sketches.move_shape: Name the tool and its action in one sentence: “I am a clamp; I squeeze the loose board so the saw cannot make it jump.”
sketches.first_card: Saw: toothed, eager, and already imagining itself the hero of the cut.

sketches.title: Repair or Ruin
sketches.premise: Something in the shed is always going wrong, and each player answers the last object with another object that can plainly fix, block, or transform it. The commentary treats every failed repair like a grand engineering tragedy involving one very overconfident child.
sketches.criterion: A move overcomes the standing object only by naming a direct repair, restraint, cut, seal, lift, or transformation, not by escaping, enduring, enlarging it, or repeating its kind without explaining the mechanism.
sketches.move_shape: Say the object and the repair it performs: “I am glue, and I seal the crack the drill has made.”
sketches.first_card: Drill: whirling, boring, and certain that every surface is an invitation.

sketches.title: Bench of Challenges
sketches.premise: The workbench hosts a chain of practical challenges: each player places one object that can directly answer the previous one. The host supplies thunderous explanations for humble victories, especially when a cloth defeats a masterpiece of machinery.
sketches.criterion: The answer must directly stop, cover, hold, cut, loosen, join, or otherwise alter the standing object’s action; a dodge, survival trick, oversized copy, or vague metaphor is a defeat for the move.
sketches.move_shape: State your object and its concrete answer: “I am a rag; I catch the oil leaking from the can.”
sketches.first_card: Oil can: slick, spilling, and dressed for a scandalous little escape.

sketches.title: Parts and Pieces
sketches.premise: Players turn the shed into a battle of useful parts: one object stands, and the next must use a different object to make its job fail. A hinge may face a nail, a wheel may face a wedge, and the host will narrate the result like the fall of an empire assembled from spare screws.
sketches.criterion: A new object wins only when its normal physical use directly blocks, separates, fastens, punctures, absorbs, or redirects the standing object; evasion, toughness, a bigger copy, and a same-family answer without a distinct action do not win.
sketches.move_shape: Name the part and its effect: “I am a wedge; I split the board the nail is trying to join.”
sketches.first_card: Nail: thin, stubborn, and loudly convinced that joining things is its destiny.

sketches.title: Shed Showdown
sketches.premise: Every turn reveals one ordinary shed thing with a job, and the next player must produce another ordinary thing whose job defeats that job. The host offers grand stage directions and a velvet-rope level of mockery for moves that merely stand nearby looking useful.
sketches.criterion: The new thing must directly interrupt, reverse, contain, remove, or transform the standing thing’s action; hiding, surviving, being too small to matter, using a bigger copy, or offering a figurative answer without a physical mechanism loses.
sketches.move_shape: Give the thing and its action: “I am a broom; I sweep the sawdust away from the drill’s work.”
sketches.first_card: Broom: bristled, sweeping, and prepared to give the floor a dramatic second act.
